This paper introduces the Time-Dependent Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (T-PARX) model, a novel framework for analyzing high-frequency count data. We demonstrate that a simple graphical comparison of sample autocorrelations and partial autocorrelations effectively guides the selection of p and q parameters in time-dependent count models. The study outlines the methodology for fitting the T-PARX model, conducts extensive simulations to evaluate its finite sample performance and inferential procedures, and applies the approach to forecast monthly goal counts in NHL and NFL games. Additionally, we develop a practical, data-driven strategy for optimizing penalty function criteria to select p, q, and exogenous covariates Xt within the model. Simulation results indicate that our iterative procedure for determining p and q outperforms alternative criteria regarding model selection criteria, autocorrelation structure preservation, and penalty function criteria. The findings from the athletic applications reveal that the data-driven optimized penalty function criteria align better with standard criteria (AIC/BIC) than direct applications, and the selected p, q, and covariate structures offer more interpretable insights compared to traditional methods. These results suggest that statistical agencies, sports organizations, and businesses can utilize this framework to extract more meaningful information from high-frequency count sequences. As these datasets grow in popularity, the proposed methodology provides a robust tool for derivation and interpretation. Furthermore, this research extends the literature on count data modeling by introducing a time-dependent generalization of the popular Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (PARX) model. Potential applications span sports analytics, economics, operations research, and public health. Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to assess the atmospheric clarity for astronomical observations appears deceptively simple, implementing it with high precision remains difficult. Over the past decade, our group has developed this technique to gauge atmospheric aerosol optical depth (AOD) using visible light photometry from 17 to 21 stars, aiming for an accuracy of $\le$0.01. This approach requires a rigorous methodology to isolate and remove the influence of stellar variability and photometric system mismatches. We have validated this technique by comparing results against established methods, such as the Lidar-derived AOD network (ATABN) and ceilometer data, as well as direct sun photometry from the US EPA AQS network and Met One ceilometers. Our measurements align well with these independent sources, achieving an average uncertainty of 0.008. Furthermore, we utilized our data to evaluate the validity of the Koschinsky backscatter factor ($\beta_{conv}$) derived from Lidar observations at the High Altitude Station at Calar Alto (HA-CA), finding significant deviations from expected values. By analyzing the correlation between $\beta_{conv}$ and AOD, we identified a gap in the standard conversion formula used to derive Mie scattering fraction ($f_{mie}$) from AOD and $\beta_{conv}$. This work details the practical application of the "photo-isolation" method for characterizing local atmospheric quality, provides the first direct observations confirming the discrepancy in $\beta_{conv}$ conversions at HA-CA, and highlights how our precise AOD data exposed an error in calculating $f_{mie}$ from simultaneous AOD and $\beta_{conv}$ readings. Additionally, we offer a concise summary of the fundamental principles behind this method. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/mahesh-k-v/Atmospheric-Photometry-CA-AA. We introduce a practical and robust implementation of Langevin dynamics for simulating crystalline and amorphous (both ordered and disordered) structures. Leveraging an efficient hybrid integrator, we demonstrate its efficacy and efficiency through simulations of simple molecular systems, comparing results directly with those obtained from standard BOMD codes like CP2K and VASP. Furthermore, we highlight the method's powerful sampling capabilities using an extensive protocol for a complex system: the drug Ritonavir, which yielded novel molecular arrangements. Finally, we outline potential applications of this approach in materials science and pharmaceutical research, emphasizing its value for structure optimization, conformational analysis, and the investigation of phase transitions and reaction mechanisms. The code is accessible at https://github.com/chenyuheng100/LD. Automated systems generating image captions are routinely assessed using human-collected reference data, such as the COCO dataset \cite{coco}, which is also employed to train these models. Given that this data serves a supervised learning role, it is crucial to ensure its representativeness across the full spectrum of image types present in the training sets of underlying neural networks. If the systems are exposed to a wider variety of images during operation than are covered by the benchmark, they may produce descriptions for underrepresented categories that diverge significantly from human norms. Such discrepancies could be misleadingly interpreted as failures of neuro linguistic linguisticistic principles by evaluators. To investigate whether COCO's coverage suffices for its intended application, we conducted a study wherein native English speakers ranked the most suitable descriptions for 500 images lacking COCO references. These 500 images were randomly selected from a dataset of 1 million images with exactly one silver reference caption per image, sourced from the EU Vision Language Challenge \footnote{http://visionlanguagechallenge.eu/}. The 500 images used for evaluation were further divided into three groups: 200 animals, 200 landscapes, and 100 events. The results indicate that images with no human reference are not necessarily superior to those with automatic descriptions when selected for use as training data. Furthermore, the specific categories of images missing COCO captions do not appear to generate systematically worse descriptions than other types. We conclude by offering recommendations for future research directions.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties of QCD matter under conditions relevant to heavy-ion collisions, with a specific focus on baryon and meson yields. While statistical models have successfully predicted hadron production in relativistic heavy-ion collisions for over two decades, they have historically relied on fixed yield ratios for specific pairs, such as $\Lambda/\pi$, $\Xi/\pi$, and $\Omega/\pi$, to achieve accuracy. In contrast, our approach employs a state-of-the-art grand canonical ensemble (GCE) model to independently predict all hadron yields. To validate this method, we first report successful predictions for specific yield ratios using recent data from Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 19.6, 27, 39, and 45 GeV at RHIC, as well as $p$+Pb and Pb+Pb collisions at various energies at the LHC. Building on this foundation, we utilize the GCE model to forecast the total baryon and meson content of vapor and liquid hadronic matter at the predicted freeze-out temperature and baryon chemical potential for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV at RHIC and 5.02 TeV at the LHC. This paper introduces the concept of integrated data and energy delivery (IDED) over single-carrier (single-carrier IDED-EE) and orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM-EE) systems for point-to-point links. It formulates and solves optimal beamforming and selection strategies to maximize data rate per unit energy consumed at the output (EE-out), aiming to optimize data throughput and data rate per unit total input energy (EE-in). The analysis reveals that for linearly dependent channels, the ideal beamforming utilizes only one antenna, confirming that no single-point solution exists where all antennas remain active. Consequently, an efficient algorithm based on sorting and bisection search is proposed to globally maximize EE-out in OFDM-EE systems without requiring iterative matrix-based calculations or specific statistical channel state information (CSI) distributions at the receiver. Numerical results demonstrate significant gains in EE-out compared to existing methods, with improvements in EE-in reaching over 100% relative to practical feasible solutions for single-point solutions. Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) represents a complex statistical challenge that demands rigorous methodological care. While recent years have seen significant advances in both the selection of fitting techniques and the development of uncertainty estimation methods, these approaches lack mathematical consistency. Specifically, the standard "Lévy" framework, which models PDFs as simple weighted histograms, fails to align with modern techniques like Tensions Measurements (TM) or when incorporating physical constraints such as sum rules. This misalignment creates issues with probability normalization and generates spurious correlations and uncertainties, particularly in the tails of distributions. To address these problems, this article introduces a unified theory framework capable of integrating all current fitting methods, sum rule constraints, and future innovative approaches. Within this framework, PDFs are treated as true probability distribution functions, and every technique is reformulated to ensure consistency and optimality. Although this theory framework does not directly yield a solution, it establishes necessary guidelines for developing a new, fully consistent and optimal Lévy framework. Potential directions for this upcoming approach are discussed. Furthermore, the framework clarifies the role of prior distributions in Bayesian methods, revealing that recent innovations like TM and Positivity Constraints function effectively as priors. Finally, this work provides consistent definitions for various uncertainty estimators, including Hessian and Monte Carlo methods, as well as recent alternatives like "What If" and Profile Likelihood uncertainties. The proposed theory framework serves as an essential foundation for future "workshops" dedicated to practical implementations. These implementation phases will require re-evaluating parton distribution parameterizations, correlation structures, and uncertainty estimators, potentially necessitating updates to global fitting projects. Such revisions could involve adopting non-linear parameterizations, as seen in the recent CT18 distribution, or utilizing data-driven forms like TM's "eigenfunction expansion." This study employs direct numerical simulations (DNS) to analyze a turbulent non-premixed jet flame subjected to transverse acoustic forcing. Within a linearized framework, the reaction to this forcing is characterized using two distinct methodologies: an image-based approach, where an unburnt gas field containing acoustic disturbances is simulated, and an active flame methodology, which linearizes the reaction against the acoustic perturbation directly on the flame front. Although these methods yield equivalent results for planar flames, the linearized image-based simulations struggle with vortex formation in jet flows due to initial velocity discontinuities, whereas the active flame approach remains viable even when the flame exhibits curvature and stretching. Consequently, the active flame framework is utilized to investigate the reaction of a linearized acoustic disturbance at the inlet of a preheat flame to local heat release oscillations induced by vortex shedding. The resulting reaction vector is integrated along the linearized acoustic path in the image to construct a global response description. This reconstruction reveals that the global response aligns precisely with the outcomes of linearized image-based simulations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the reaction to inlet acoustic oscillations in a stretched, linearized preheat flame depends significantly on its local Karlovitz number ($\mathbf{Ka}$), oscillating for low $\mathbf{Ka}$ values ($\mathbf{Ka}<1$) and displaying a peak amplitude near $\mathbf{Ka}=1$, while exhibiting negligible reaction for higher $\mathbf{Ka}$ values. These findings offer valuable insights for developing response models in turbulent combustion systems, particularly in linearized flame response modeling, and support the hypothesis that thermal noise in jet flames originates from the reaction to velocity fluctuations when the local Karlovitz number is approximately unity. Additionally, these results support the observation that the stabilization of counter rotating vortices in premixed jets post-acoustic actuation corresponds to a region of high acoustic velocity, which drives a shift in the mean flow velocity. Ultimately, this research confirms that DNS, coupled with linearized analysis, serves as a potent tool for dissecting vortex dynamics induced by acoustic forcing in turbulent jets. Such investigations are crucial for validating linearized models, including Proper Gas Dynamic Modes (PGMs), which rely on initial conditions derived from the reaction to acoustic actuation, and for clarifying the mechanisms behind thermo-acoustic instabilities observed in laboratory experiments. Ultimately, these linearized models and associated DNS simulations provide essential theoretical foundations for understanding the complex interactions between thermo-acoustic instabilities and vortex dynamics in practical gas turbine engines.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the success of nonlocality in other physical fields. Although mathematically consistent, NLG lacks a established constitutive framework and has not been applied to cosmic evolution or gravitational wave propagation. This work introduces a constitutive framework for nonlocal gravity, drawing parallels with electrodynamics, and investigates its impact on cosmic evolution and gravitational wave dynamics using both analytical methods and numerical simulations. The findings reveal that the constitutive model determines the speed of gravitational wave propagation within an anisotropic nonlocal gravity environment. Furthermore, an anisotropic nonlocal constitutive relationship accelerates cosmic expansion, whereas an isotropic model decelerates it; under specific conditions, this acceleration can even surpass the prediction of the $\Lambda$-term in general relativity. These outcomes highlight the significance of material science perspectives when addressing cosmic evolution and gravitational waves within the nonlocal gravity framework. Additionally, this research provides the first examination of cosmic evolution and gravitational wave dynamics within a nonlocal classical field theory, offering insights potentially transferable to other nonlocal theories such as nonlocal strong or weak interactions. The proposed constitutive framework for nonlocal gravity may also prove valuable for analyzing gravitational waves and cosmic evolution in other nonlocal field theories, including nonlocal classical theories of matter. While proton-proton collisions are characterized by low energy density and high entropy, they generate an extensive spectrum of rare, high-mass particles. These events constitute a minor system, representing approximately 0.1% of occurrences at center-of-mass energies of 13 TeV. This paper provides an overview of the most significant rare processes detectable at proton-proton colliders, beginning with a summary of LHC experimental capabilities for analyzing specific final states. It then details the primary processes responsible for producing the WZ, ZZ, and tZ(t)() systems, as well as other relevant contributions. Finally, we present current limits on various diphoton + jet + E_T missing events and outline promising directions for future research. These rare processes offer ideal laboratories for investigating physics within the Standard Model at high energies and for searching for new phenomena, serving as ideal test cases for future high-luminance colliders. At future hadron machines, the priority will shift from measuring cross-sections to uncovering novel physics; for instance, the High-Luminosity LHC will enhance sensitivity to new resonances by a factor of ten, and the High-Energy HL-LHC could potentially discover new particles with masses up to 4.5 times that of the Higgs boson. At fixed-target baryon-baryon colliders like the AFTER@LHC experiment, new resonances will be produced on purpose, on-shell, with high cross-sections. This document also offers an overview of searches for exotic hadrons at the LHC, highlighting recent findings and future prospects. At these low energy density, high-entropy collisions, most hadron-hadron interactions result in semi-inclusive or fully inclusive events characterized by the production of few particles accompanied by large hadronic activity, often failing to trigger detectors or providing limited utility for studying new particle searches. Consequently, this will be a primary challenge for future baryon-baryon colliders: distinguishing genuine exotic signals from background. Fortunately, events with exactly two or zero jets and missing transverse energy will receive dedicated attention at baryon-baryon colliders, as these final states will be ideal for searching for new particles. In contrast, at the LHC and other proton-proton colliders, identifying new resonances in the dijet mass spectrum remains the most effective strategy for discovering particles with masses exceeding a few times the beam energy. This paper concludes with an update on the search for new particles in the dijet mass spectrum at the LHC, discussing recent results

We address the significance of rare, long-duration outbursts from Galactic X-ray binary systems, specifically those exceeding a year without detection, to clarify the characteristics of the six systems in the Galactic Centre and the feasibility of identifying an active black hole. Firstly, we contend that the concept of a "duty cycle" is unsuitable for describing the variability of X-ray transients in the context of gravitational wave searches. Secondly, applying a Poisson distribution to the Galactic Centre systems reveals that having no detected transient in the last three years is statistically improbable if the system ensemble were truly variable. Thirdly, we propose that the accretion onto the compact object in the Galactic Centre follows a "clumpy" model, where a finite number of discrete events occur annually. Under this model, the total mass gained accounts for the required mass-to-luminosity ratio, with individual clumps responsible for X-ray outbursts. Finally, when examining neutron star systems to identify potential sources for the GWski or GWski-1 events, we find that the accretion timescales derived from previous studies for the system associated with GWski-1 are inconsistent with the observed rise time. This discrepancy suggests an initial peak luminosity higher than currently estimated, implying that the standard inference of accretion timescale from luminosity and mass accretion rate may be flawed. Consequently, we suggest that the activity of this system, as well as that of other systems with prolonged quiescent periods, cannot be simply modeled as a constant rate over the relevant observation window. These conclusions carry significant implications for analyzing such systems during gravitational wave searches. Ultimately, we determine that a black hole is likely responsible for the variability observed in the Galactic Centre. If present, this black hole has probably never formed a transient detectable by X-ray telescopes, thereby explaining why no such event has been seen thus far. A graph $G$ admits a clean characterization as a subgraph of a completely split Kneser graph $K_n^{2,1}$ if and only if $G$ is a subgraph of the complete graph $K_n$. This paper introduces a FPT algorithm deciding whether a specific bipartite graph $G$ can be embedded into $K_n^{2,1}$. Additionally, if such an embedding exists, the algorithm constructs the corresponding realization within $K_n^{2,1}$. The problem of determining if a graph $G$ is a subgraph of $K_n^{2,1}$ is equivalent to verifying if the "doubly split expanded graph" of $G$ (denoted as $H$) is feasible as a complete $3$-partite graph with specified degree constraints across its parts. Deciding the feasibility of such graphs involves solving a system of linear equations subject to integer and bound restrictions on variables. Furthermore, constructing the actual realization requires addressing integer programming tasks. This algorithm utilizes an exact formula to identify potential locations for entries equal to $1$ and verifies these candidates using linear algebraic methods. High-performance applications frequently exceed the throughput capabilities of current CPUs, a limitation we address by introducing HyperDegrade. This technique enables programs that surpass CPU speed limits to run faster by executing selected computational kernels at higher frequencies using hardware voltage frequency scaling (VFS). HyperDegrade dynamically balances workload execution speeds and performance through an online, iterative algorithm that optimizes overall performance without missing deadlines. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that HyperDegrade outperforms existing real-time scheduling methods, meeting all deadlines while achieving up to 2.7x greater performance gain than state-of-the-art workload schedulers. Furthermore, our results confirm that HyperDegrade surpasses theoretical performance limits established by static workloads. These findings indicate that workloads utilizing HyperDegrade can exceed the performance gains possible with static voltage frequency scaling (e.g., running all workloads at maximum frequency), particularly when workloads are heterogeneous and have varying performance requirements at different frequencies. To support these evaluations, we released the open-source system "Voltnomist," which dynamically prioritizes workloads executing at frequencies above their normal operating points. Source code for both HyperDegrade and Voltnomist is accessible at https://github.com/ntucci/HyperDegrade and https://github.com/ntucci/Voltnomist, respectively.

We introduce a novel unknotting move called the swipte, which combines the crossing change and the twist operations. We demonstrate that adding a swipte unknot to a welded link yields a equivalent link under the $\bar{\Delta}$-move, while for classical links, the result becomes equivalent under full twists. Consequently, two classical or welded links related by a swipte unknot crossing are equivalent provided they are also equivalent without the swipte unknot. We prove that any classical link can be transformed into a plat or bracket link via a sequence of Reimer moves, crossing changes, and swiptes, offering an alternative approach to deciding if a classical link is split. Furthermore, we show that for both classical and welded links, the composition of two swiptes is equivalent to a Redmond move. This implies that a diagrammatic invariant remains constant across all such invariants for classical and welded links. We define the new invariant by generalizing Kauffman's bracket invariant for classical links to the swipte invariant. We also generalize this to the fundamental invariant for welded links, extending it to invariants of classical links and a disentangling invariant for link groups. Specifically, we generalize the isotopy invariant of the fundamental group of classical links to that of the fundamental group of welded links. As an application, we introduce a new disentangling operation for welded links and present an algorithm to convert a welded link diagram into an equivalent classical link diagram, minimizing self-crossings. We conclude by introducing additional operators on classical and welded links and proposing open questions regarding these structures. The formalism developed here may prove useful for analyzing knotted tubes formed from hoses, cables, ropes, and similar objects. Supporting files include a video of the new unknotting move and an implementation of the algorithm for converting welded links to classical links in Open CASCADE Technology. The code and video are accessible at https://github.com/AnatolyVdovin/Swipte.

This game theoretic study examines how two teams of agents play a signal detection game on regular graphs to determine whether an attack occurs, all while minimizing their own energy usage. The agents' strategies are grounded in limited detection capabilities and rely on point functions derived from Bayesian game theory. In an effort to balance energy consumption with detection performance, the teams deploy sensing and communication strategies that are as uniform as possible across the graph's nodes, utilizing either sleep-wake or multi-task prioritization approaches. We analyze a game where the defending team anticipates the attacking team's detection strategy, comparing the optimal Nash equilibrium strategies for both limited and unconstrained energy levels. Our work details the construction of these equilibrium strategies, formulates mathematical programs to optimize energy consumption while meeting minimum detection requirements, and investigates the impact of energy constraints on equilibrium detection outcomes. Specifically, we focus on 3-regular graphs, extending our analysis to 4- and 5-regular graphs in the appendix. Through this examination, we derive explicit expressions for the energy required by the attacking team to maintain undetected operations and for the defending team to locate attackers when undetected attacking strategies are considered. Our findings reveal that, under certain conditions, increasing the energy available to either team can paradoxically worsen the detection probability of undetected attacking strategies. The derived formulations and expressions are applicable to various optimization challenges involving games on regular graphs, such as resource allocation, spectrum sharing, and sensor network deployments. Ultimately, this research provides a foundational framework for games where rational participants prioritize hierarchical objectives, such as detecting and locating threats, alongside other goals like avoiding detection themselves. These models are particularly relevant for competitive scenarios like military operations, cybersecurity competitions, and adversarial machine learning. Ultimately, we hope this study inspires further investigation into games of multi-task prioritization on regular graphs, particularly regarding the detection of undetected strategies and the optimization of resource allocation among different activities. Such optimization is driven by the assumption that agents with finite energy will distribute it among tasks to maximize utility, a concept directly mirrored in our game by the attacking team's goal of remaining undetected and the defending team's aim of locating these specific undetected strategies.

Although current generations of high-power gravitational-wave detectors (GWDs) achieve remarkable sensitivity at most frequencies, they struggle at high frequencies ($f_{HF}$), limiting the detection of significant high-frequency gravitational waves (e.g., from binary neutron star mergers). This limitation stems from shot noise, whose impact worsens as frequency increases in standard interferometer architectures. To overcome this, we propose a new sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (SSI) design, potentially realizable with upgraded 4km-scale LIGO, KAGRA, or Virgo detectors. Utilizing extra beamsplitter(s) and a closed light loop, the SSI dynamically adjusts the operating point of arms functioning as interferometers, thereby shifting shot noise effects across different frequencies. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that an updated LIGO Hanover could see its high-frequency sensitivity ($f_{HF} > 250$ Hz) improve by over an order of magnitude. Furthermore, a hybrid sloshing-Sagnac configuration combining two LIGO Hanover detectors with one KAGRA detector might exhibit a "10-fold narrow-bandsensitive" pattern around binary neutron star merger frequencies. Distinct from the typical $\sqrt{N}$-limited sensitivity curve, this pattern features a deep narrow-band noise dip, attributable to the constructive interference of shot noise between the baselines of two SSI units (an effect also potentially achievable with two conventional interferometers via a external lightsplitter). Such a dip could enable the precise identification of previously undetected gravitational wave signals buried within noise. Soccer teams tend to adopt risk-averse strategies when facing a deficit, particularly in the final stages of a match. This phenomenon suggests that agents operating in such contexts can achieve success by taking bolder actions. However, when a team finds itself trailing with little time remaining, players and coaches often struggle to determine the most effective responses. Similarly, automatic decision-making systems, including those based on reinforcement learning (RL), may struggle in these high-pressure scenarios due to the scarcity of rewarding experiences available for specific actions. To address this challenge, we introduce a contextual action context network (CCAN) designed to assist deep reinforcement learning models in selecting optimal actions within critical soccer moments. Building on this, we propose a hybrid approach that combines CCAN with asymptotic value iteration (AVI), a classical method. Extensive experiments conducted across two distinct datasets demonstrate that our proposed AVI-CCAN framework significantly outperforms both traditional baseline methods and state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The source code for this project is accessible at: https://github.com/yuhengbo/Contextual_Action_Context.

Although deep learning has achieved remarkable success in classification tasks, there remains no consensus on which loss function yields optimal results. This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of common loss functions—specifically cross-entropy, Poisson, negative binomial, and hinge loss—across 27 public datasets. The assessment covers both over- and under-fitted models, analyzed individually and in ensemble configurations, using statistical metrics, visual inspections, and calibration plots. Findings indicate that for under-fitted models, cross-entropy generally produces the best outcomes. However, when balancing over- and under-fitting, Poisson and negative binomial losses often outperform other options. Notably, switching from mean to Huber loss in hinge loss significantly degrades performance if the dataset exhibits class imbalance or when statistical measures like MAE and MSE are high. Ultimately, no single loss function is universally superior; the choice should be guided by the specific characteristics of the dataset and the relevant error metrics. Furthermore, simply increasing model complexity or hyperparameter tuning without selecting an appropriate loss function for the data's characteristics yields limited improvements. Furthermore, recent approaches lacking physical remain robust to additive noise but remain insensitive to linear or nonlinear distortions caused by variations in stethoscope characteristics or recording devices. Our method involves normalizing heart sound recordings to mitigate variations in acoustic gain and device type, followed by convolving a noise kernel with the normalized sounds to learn filter weights invariant to specific noise characteristics. These weights are then applied to construct 2D image-like representations of heart sounds, which are analyzed by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier. It remains uncertain if a double-slope break on the mass-to-lightness conversion along the Mendelson-Farrah curve is genuine. To investigate this, we examined stellar population models incorporating nits—low lightness regions driven by low velocity gradients—within the most massive galaxies. Our findings indicate that at high masses, these low lightness zones substantially increase the mass-to-lightness ratio, accounting for the slope change observed above Log($M_*$) = 10.9. We conclude that the turning over of the specific star formation rate (sSFR) at high masses, depicted in Figure 1, likely results from this slope shift in the mass-to-lightness rather than a physical drop in star formation efficiency. The presence of nits in the most massive galaxies aligns with the prediction that low lightness regions emerge where self-gravity surpasses gas vertical support. Furthermore, these nits may help preserve low specific gas surface densities by preventing gas density from rising when central accumulations occur, thereby avoiding the "misfire" of starbursts. This mechanism could explain why even the most massive galaxies have not evolved into true ellipticals. These processes offer a unified account for various non-linear trends in the most massive galaxies, including the M*-B relation, the Log(sSFR)-M* relation, and the N(UHI)-M* relation. Finally, we argue that nits represent a crucial link between low specific gas surface densities and high central gas surface densities.

This study reports on the X-ray properties of the ultra-fast rotating HerX-1, a low-mass X-ray binary with a 49.59 $\pm$ 0.30 second period. While the 2--10 keV unabsorbed luminosity remained consistently around $3 \times 10^{32}$ W throughout the 2019/2020 observations, the variable cross between the total luminosity and unabsorbed flux indicated that variability extended into the soft band below 2 keV. A hard/soft state transition was not detected during these campaigns. Analysis of timing properties revealed that both Positive and Negative QPO pairs persisted across a narrow range of 27--29 Hz, remaining stable over the course of the observations. Furthermore, the power spectral density displayed a broad stochastic noise spectrum featuring a distinct "bump" at approximately 0.6 Hz, a feature previously linked to higher accretion rates in other systems. When compared to the mass--outflow relation established by  aton et al. (2020), HerX-1 appears to possess mass loss rates that are anomalously high for its low luminosity. Potential explanations for this anomaly include non-standard angular momentum transport, the recent ingestion of a companion planet, or an underestimation of the system's mass due to an inclination angle greater than 80 degrees. The persistent qnub+ and qnu- frequencies align with predictions from the $r$-mode instability curve, whereas the spin frequency and its evolution trend are consistent with a low mass accretion rate curve. Various theoretical models predicting frequency correlations as a function of accretion rate were also evaluated against the observed properties of HerX-1. Additionally, simplified accretion disk models were simulated to test whether the observed spectrum could be reproduced, ultimately suggesting that a standard model alone is insufficient to account for all characteristics of HerX-1. These findings collectively indicate that the accretion flow in this system deviates significantly from expectations for a system of its specific mass and accretion rate. Potential causes for this deviation are discussed in detail. Finally, the possibility of detecting r-mode oscillations in the accretion disk of an ultra-short period binary is also considered. Synthetic data serves as a crucial resource for developing algorithms tailored to underrepresented datasets, such as brain MRI scans. Despite its significance, existing methods fall short when applied to specific medical domains. We introduce a novel framework designed to generate brain injury images from brain MRI scans. This framework builds upon a conditional progressive GAN (CGAN) and a variational auto-encoder (VAE), utilizing a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, a brain injury VAE-CGAN processes normal brain images to create synthetic normal brain images and learn latent representations of healthy brains. During the second stage, the model trains on images depicting brain injuries to develop new latent representations and produce corresponding injury images. As a regression task, we evaluate the realism of the generated images using the Frechet Inception Score (FIS) and Mean Squared Error (MSE). Furthermore, as a classification task, we employ support vector machines (SVM) to distinguish between real and synthetic images, as well as to classify different types of brain injuries from the synthetic datasets. Application on both T1 and T2 MRI datasets yields an MSE of 0.0002 and a FIS of 63.11 on T1, and an MSE of 0.0003 with a FIS of 59.09 on T2. The SVM achieves 99.9% accuracy in discriminating real from fake T1 images and 99.8% on T2 images, while also reaching 99.9% accuracy in identifying specific brain injury types from T1 data and 99.2% from T2 data. These results indicate that our framework effectively generates high-quality, realistic-sounding synthetic brain injury images. Additionally, we developed a mobile application capable of detecting brain injuries from T1 and T2 scans without requiring specialized medical expertise. This solution offers significant value for developing nations and regions lacking access to advanced medical technology or expert personnel. Automated testing serves as a crucial technique for enhancing the reliability of C/C++ code, yet existing solutions fall short in guaranteeing that a sufficient range of executions is covered to uncover specific errors. Our geometric method addresses this gap by initially constructing a dependency graph from the source code to divide execution possibilities into distinct geometric regions. The system then autonomously selects and runs test cases designed to explore as many of these regions as feasible. Implementing this approach required significant optimizations to a constraint solver, which manages the coordinates of data types like integers and arrays within each region to ensure valid accesses. We integrated this solution into the CUTE tester, adding support for C++11. Evaluations using industry-standard C++11 codebases demonstrate that our optimized solver outperforms prior constraint solvers and that CUTE effectively covers diverse execution spaces, identifying over 10,000 errors in just 18 hours across two real-world projects. Available at https://github.com/microsoft/CUTE, the source code supports both our novel method and the ability to utilize previous versions of CUTE alongside external dependency graphs for testing. Comparative assessments confirm that our solver is significantly faster when combined with traditional code-dependent methods for generating regression tests from error reports or manual inputs. Additionally, a specialized integration of our method with an error detection tool (Clang-Static-Analyzer) successfully identified numerous errors that standard approaches missed. These findings indicate that automating the generation of regression tests from errors—isolating the faulty code from context—works effectively with our method, whereas it was unfeasible using earlier combinations of execution context isolation and testing techniques. Ultimately, our system provides a practical solution for massively increasing the volume of regression tests required to verify that fixes for one set of errors do not introduce or fail to address other issues. These new techniques achieve the fastest known constant-time complexity for exact matrix inversion: O(n2/3) for BDCI and O(n0.75) for BDCI-Gen, where n represents the matrix order. Furthermore, we establish that BDCI-Gen is approximately 8 times faster than CI for a 10,240-order matrix. We developed a hydrodynamical simulation to examine how dust evolution influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) within protoplanetary disks. Our results indicate that while gas settling enhances VSI growth rates in absence of dust evolution, the formation of pebbles in the meter-size gap ultimately suppresses this instability by reducing vertical gradients. Furthermore, we found that VSI-driven turbulence facilitates dust evolution by accelerating settling and promoting local dust concentration through instabilities arising in the radial direction. Finally, we assessed the validity of the hydrodynamical approximation by comparing our simulations with linear wave theory. Our analysis reveals that in outer regions, the VSI wavelength exceeds the local sound crossing time, rendering the hydrodynamical simulation reliable for these areas. However, in inner regions, the wavelength falls below the sound crossing time, causing the hydrodynamical approach to fail. These wavelength variations also account for differences in growth rates between inner and outer regions; specifically, the VSI growth rate in the inner regions is slower than expected due to the instability operating on shorter wavelength modes. These conclusions rely on standard dust evolution models, suggesting that further research is necessary to determine if similar mechanisms apply under alternative evolution scenarios. Ultimately, our study highlights that both the specific dust evolution model and the local gas surface density are critical factors in VSI development, with the instability tending to be stronger in regions exhibiting lower gas surface densities and less advanced dust evolution.

This paper addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across Edge Devices (EDs) with non-independent and non-identical distributions in a Federated Learning (FL) setting, where EDs communicate with the PS over potentially slow and unreliable links. This study introduces a novel consistency regularization framework tailored for pixel-level semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The approach begins by generating initial segmentations for unlabeled data using a teacher network trained on both supervised and unsupervised datasets. These predictions are then incorporated as additional loss terms to optimize the model on the unlabeled portion. Distinguishing itself from existing methods, our framework employs a combination of mean squared error, masking, and category-wise entropy losses. Specifically, the mean squared error loss is applied only to pixels with high confidence, as indicated by the entropy loss, while the masking loss focuses optimization efforts on under-segmented regions identified via mean integer value predictions. Extensive experiments conducted across two public datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robustness against noise in pixel labels and requires minimal human intervention, as it needs no manual thresholding for segmentation masking or weight assignment for mean integer value weighting. In this work, we demonstrate that the resource of genuinely nonlocality within a scenario is precisely what is required to perform genuinely nonlocal tasks, such as violating a Bell inequality or executing a specifically defined task, given the access to single-particle entanglement. Specifically, we show that a genuinely nonlocal effect derived from a Mermin-Klyshko (MK) inequality allows for violating any other MK inequality of the same order. Furthermore, we establish that single-particle entanglement can also yield genuinely nonlocal effects, a phenomenon we term "single-particle steering." Consequently, this implies that genuinely nonlocal effects like those described by MK inequalities can be utilized to detect single-particle steering. Finally, we provide an experimental verification of these findings using photonic states. These results highlight that single-particle entanglement, when employed in scenarios involving genuinely nonlocal effects, functions analogously to EPR pairs; similarly, the resource of single-particle steering serves the same purpose as a genuinely nonlocal effect (such as an MK inequality) in scenarios where genuinely nonlocal behaviors, behaviors conditioned on single-particle entanglement, and behaviors conditioned on single-particle steering are exhibited. We conclude by outlining the practical applications of these discoveries.

Although Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have achieved significant success in various domains, their substantial memory requirements and computational complexity often limit practical deployment, particularly in hardware settings for video analysis. Subsequently, we apply a hierarchical tucker (HT) decomposition during the algorithmic phase to compress the video's tensor representation and optimize weights and biases within the LSTM. On the hardware side, we designed a specialized HT-decomposition circuit and a dedicated circuit for processing pre-filtered video tensors. These circuits enable real-time on-the-fly compression and expansion, eliminating the need for extra memory for weight or video storage. Evaluations using public video datasets demonstrate that a network utilizing our algorithm and hardware co-design requires 99.17 GB less memory for weights and 2.27 GB less for video data compared to a standard architecture with identical HT decomposition orders. Hardware simulations on Synopsys Design Compiler with the 28-nm technology node reveal that the co-designed architecture operates 1.39× faster, accessing 75.72× less memory per frame than a conventional LSTM network. Finally, real-time deployments on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 platform for video identification tasks confirm the validity of our algorithm and hardware co-design strategy. The corresponding open-source code and simulations are accessible at: https://github.com/HTLSTM/HTLSTM.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors representing the most prevalent method for evaluating hypotheses through the calculation of evidence. Although Bayes factors offer a compelling alternative to p-values as a direct measure of support for hypotheses rather than a metric of error probabilities, they are susceptible to criticism similar to that directed at significance testing. Specifically, the influence of nuisance parameters and prior probabilities can render Bayes factors unstable and difficult to interpret. While researchers have historically avoided these complications by employing cutoff values to treat Bayes factors like p-values, such an approach neglects the granular information Bayes factors provide. Instead of relying on thresholds, we should focus on strategies for selecting appropriate priors within Bayesian analysis. This paper reviews the relationship between Bayes factors and likelihood ratios, evaluates methods for addressing the issues causing criticism of Bayes factors, and proposes workflow-oriented solutions. These workflows enable the utilization of multiple prior sets to overcome challenges associated with nuisance parameters and the sensitivity of Bayes factors to prior probabilities, thereby allowing for more robust statistical inference.

This study presents a novel inverse problem involving the 3D reconstruction of an excitation source for a passive acoustic structure. The experimental setup consists of a loudspeaker illuminating a finite plate, with vibrations measured by an array of laser vibrometers. An inverse operator is constructed by integrating a forward model of the excitations with a structural acoustic model to predict vibration amplitudes at specific locations. To reconstruct the excitation, this operator is applied to the recorded vibration data using deconvolution. Regularization is implemented to ensure a physically realistic solution, achieved through a novel formulation that enforces both local smoothness and global energy conservation. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on two distinct source types: a localized "punctual" excitation and a global "sine sweep" input. Results from single- and multi-position experiments, along with reconstruction quality assessments, are reported. Finally, the method's utility is highlighted for identifying anomalies in the excitation, such as unintended simultaneous activations of multiple loudspeakers. The underlying regularized operator splitting algorithm is highly efficient and easily adaptable to other inverse problems in structural acoustic interactions.
